text: An Intrusion Detection System and an Intrusion Prevention System often run the exact same detection logic underneath. The difference that actually matters for a SOC is where each one sits on the network, and what it's allowed to do the moment it finds something bad — one can only ever tell you about it, the other can act.

An IDS is a passive sensor. It doesn't sit in the direct path between two segments — a switch is configured to send it a copy of the traffic, usually through a SPAN port (a Switched Port Analyzer) or a dedicated network tap. The IDS inspects that copy out of band, and when something matches its detection logic, all it can do is raise an alert. By the time that alert fires, the original packet has already been delivered.

An IPS runs much of that same logic, but it's deployed inline, physically or logically placed directly in the path the traffic has to travel, the same way a firewall is. Every packet passes through the IPS before it's allowed to continue. When the IPS matches something malicious, it can drop the packet, reset the connection, or block the source in real time, stopping the traffic before it ever reaches its target.

That inline position is also the IPS's biggest liability. Because it sits directly in the traffic's path, a false positive isn't just a noisy alert — it's a real outage, blocking legitimate traffic until someone finds and fixes the rule. An IDS can never cause that kind of outage, since it never touches the live packet, but that safety has a cost: it cannot stop an attack already in progress. That's exactly why many teams deploy a brand-new rule in IDS mode first, confirm its false-positive rate is low against real traffic, and only then flip it to IPS mode to let it actually block.

Next up, the other major split in how detection logic actually works: signature-based rules that match known attack patterns with speed and precision, versus anomaly-based detection that baselines what's normal and flags anything that deviates from it.
